title: 大阪・名古屋・東京 30℃以上予想
body:
今日21日は暖かい南よりの風で気温が上がるでしょう。最高気温は名古屋で32℃、大阪や東京都心は30℃の予想で、もし30℃以上になると統計開始以来、最も遅い真夏日になりそうです。ただ、次第に寒気が流れ込むため、夜は朝よりもヒンヤリする所が多いでしょう。服装でうまく調節してください。
今日21日は、低気圧が急速に発達しながら日本海から北海道の北へ進み、前線が本州付近を通過するでしょう。低気圧や前線に向かって暖かい南よりの風が強まり、雨の所でも平年を上回る気温となりそうです。最高気温は、九州南部から関東で30℃以上の真夏日になる所があるでしょう。名古屋は32℃、高知は31℃、大阪と東京都心は30℃の予想で、もし30℃以上になれば統計開始以来、最も遅い真夏日になります。喉が渇く前に水分をとり、無理をせず、こまめに休憩をとるよう心がけてください。
前線通過後は次第に寒気が流れ込むため、気温の変化が大きくなるでしょう。札幌は午後9時に13℃くらい、深夜0時には10℃を下回る予想です。福岡は午前5時過ぎに25.6℃を観測していて、日中は気温が下がってくるでしょう。次第に北または西よりの風に変わるため、実際の気温よりもヒンヤリと感じられそうです。関東も北部から北よりの風に変わりますが、南部では夜も南風の入る所が多いでしょう。東京都心は夜も気温があまり下がらず、ムシムシと感じられるかもしれません。
上の図は、朝・昼・夜の服装の目安です。日中は、沖縄や九州南部、四国から関東、北陸は半袖やノースリーブなどでちょうど良いくらいでしょう。夜は、カーディガンや薄手のジャケットが必要になる所が多く、札幌はトレンチコートや厚手の上着が活躍しそうです。服装指数は、朝晩や日中の予想気温からどのような服装が適しているか提案するものです。人により暑さや寒さの感じ方が異なりますが、服装選びの参考にしてください。

title: 支援金の対象者の案 首相が答弁
body:
高市内閣が今国会の最重要法案に位置付ける消費税減税・支援金法案は２０日、衆院本会議で趣旨説明と質疑が行われ、審議入りした。焦点の一つである支援金の対象者について、高市首相は諸外国の類似の制度をあてはめた場合として「年収３５０万円」を上限とし、約２０００万人に支給する案に言及し、「一つの参考とし、国会での審議も十分踏まえつつ検討する」と述べた。【写真】高市首相の愛車だったスープラ
法案は２０２７年４月から２年間、食料品の消費税率を８％から１％に引き下げ、２９年度に「就業者負担軽減支援金」を本格導入することが柱となる。政府・与党は１１月上旬までに衆院を通過させ、１２月１２日までの会期内の成立を目指す。
首相は本会議で、消費税減税について、市場の信認を確保する観点などから「２年後には責任を持って確実に税率を元に戻す」と訴え、仮に首相が交代しても「現在の与党の首相であれば、同様の対応になる」と強調した。
経済への影響を考慮して減税を延長する場合、衆院解散に踏み切るかどうかを問われると、「景気を理由に延期することは考えていないため、国民に信を問うことは想定していない」と明言した。大規模災害や感染症の大流行があれば、「臨機応変に判断していくべきだ」とも付け加えた。
支援金は、２７、２８年度には消費税率１％相当分（年６０００億円）で先行実施する。法案では、本格導入後も含めて対象者や支給額は示されていない。政府は本会議に先立ち、与野党に対し、先行実施の対象者とする年収の下限として、社会保険料の負担が生じてきたことを考慮して「１０６万円」案を軸とし、給与所得控除を超える「７４万円」、雇用保険の加入基準の「５３万円」の２案も選択肢として示した。対象を「年収１００万～３５０万円」とすれば、約２０００万人に平均年３万円程度を支給することも例示した。
首相は、年収の上限額について「現段階で特定の額を念頭に置いているわけではない」とし、対象者の決定には「最新のデータに基づいた分析、精査を行う必要がある」と説明した。
参院では与党が過半数に４議席足りておらず、政府・与党は野党の賛成も得て法案の成立を図る考えだ。

title: SpaceXとテスラ 経営統合を検討
body: 米実業家イーロン・マスク氏は20日、自身が率いる米宇宙開発企業スペースXと米電気自動車（EV）大手テスラの経営統合の可能性を検討する特別委員会を設置したと明らかにした。欧米メディアが伝えた。マスク氏は両社の統合について「良いアイデア」と発言した。【写真まとめ】夜空に次々と現れたスターリンク衛星のフレア◇「シンギュラリティーの段階にある」この日のスペースXの決算説明会で言及した。報道によると、マスク氏は人工知能（AI）について「（人間の知能を超える）シンギュラリティーの段階にある」とした上で、両社の統合で得られるものは多いとの認識を示した。経営統合は「良いアイデアだと思うが、最終的には株主が支持しなければならない」と述べ、委員会はまだ合意に至っていないと強調した。◇マスク氏自身は議論に参加せずテスラ側は投票した株主だけでなく、全株主の50％の賛成票が必要になると指摘し、「かなり高いハードルだ」とした。マスク氏自身は利害関係にある当事者であるため、いずれの取締役会の議論にも参加していないという。【ワシントン浅川大樹】

title: 車が歩道に突っ込む 歩行者が死亡
body: 20日午後3時10分ごろ、神奈川県横須賀市野比2丁目の国道で、乗用車が歩道に突っ込み、歩いていた70代の男性に衝突した後で電柱にぶつかった。男性と乗用車を運転していた女性（79）が病院に運ばれたが、男性は搬送先の病院で死亡が確認された。女性は命に別条はなかった。【図】75歳以上ドライバー、実車試験合格なのに事故多く神奈川県警横須賀南署によると、現場は片側1車線の直線。女性が運転する乗用車が、ガードレールがない歩道を歩いていた男性に背後から衝突したという。署は、女性の回復を待って当時の状況を聞く方針。（関ゆみん）

title: 重機吊り上げ中に車に挟まれ 死亡
body: 20日午後3時49分ごろ、茨城県境町伏木の中古自動車販売会社「アハマド　ラザ　トレーディング」敷地内で、荷下ろし作業をしていたパキスタン国籍で同県古河市、会社役員、男性(55)が、ユニック車と隣に駐車したトラックの間に挟まれ、外傷性窒息で搬送先の病院で死亡が確認された。県警境署で事故原因を調べている。同署によると、トラックに積まれた重機を男性がユニック車のクレーンを操作して吊り上げたところ、男性のユニック車がバランスを崩して傾いた。

title: 米大統領 ウに露との和平合意促す
body: Steve Holland　Trevor Hunnicutt[ワシントン　２０日　ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は２０日、ロシアとの戦争終結に向け、ウクライナに和平合意に応‌じるよう求めた。トランプ氏はホワイトハウスの大統⁠領執務室で記者団に対し、「ウクライナはこの戦争を終わらせたいと望まなければならない」と述べた。また、「​ウクライナがこの戦争を終わらせるときが来た」とし、ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領が‌合意に応じることを望んでいると語った。その上で、ロシアは戦場で優位に立っているとの認識を表明。「ロシアは巨大‌な機械のようなもので、た‌だ前進し続けており、実際にそうしてき​た」とし、「ロシアは非常に広い領土を占領した」と述べた。トランプ氏はまた、‌ロシアで拘束されている米国人の元教師、スティーブン・ハバード氏の問題に‌ついて、ロシアのプーチン​大統領と協議したと明らかにし、この件につ‌いて近く進展がある可能性を示唆した。トランプ氏は、ハバード氏に関する⁠記者団の質問に対し「プーチン氏とこの件について話をしている」とし、「何が起きるか見ていてほしい。われわれはハバード氏の問題に集中⁠して取り組んできた」と述べた。ハバード氏は７４歳​で、傭兵活動に関‌する罪で有罪判決を受けロシアの刑務所で約７年の刑に服している。米国務省はハバード氏の件を不当拘束と認定している。ゼレンスキー⁠大統領はこの日、ノルウェーの首都オスロで米国⁠のウィットコフ和平交渉担当特使と会談。会談後の記者会見で、ロシア⁠による弾道ミサイル攻撃に関する情報共有や早期警戒の提供を米国が再開したこ‌とに⁠謝意を示した。ノルウェーのストーレ首相によると、ウィット​コフ氏は２１日にロシア第２の都市サンクトペテルブルクを訪問し、ロシア首脳部と会談する。

title: 露の道新記者拘束 米国務省が非難
body:
【ワシントン共同】米国務省の報道担当者は19日、ロシア当局がスパイ容疑で北海道新聞の記者を拘束したことを巡り「ジャーナリストや独立した意見を持つ人々に対する威嚇や嫌がらせ、処罰などのいかなる試みも非難する」と述べた。スパイ行為を否定する日本側を擁護した。共同通信の取材に答えた。【写真】「ロシア兵器9割に日本部品」　ミサイルや無人機に転用　名指しされた日本企業13社
報道担当者は「米国は表現の自由を基本的な権利と考えている。社会は自由な意見の表明により強化され、自由な社会での政府による検閲は容認できない」と訴えた。記者は13日、ウクライナへの「特別軍事作戦」に北方領土と千島列島から動員された兵士の数の情報を日本の情報機関の指示で収集したとしてロシア連邦保安局（FSB）に拘束された。

title: 米政権の汚職問題 中間選挙争点に
body:
間近に迫った米中間選挙の新たな争点にトランプ政権の「corruption（汚職、腐敗）」問題が急浮上している。最近の各種世論調査で、有権者がインフレやイラン戦争などより汚職問題を最も懸念していることが判明。メディアはこぞってこの話題を取り上げ、民主党は政権の汚職体質を有権者に訴える選挙CMを流し始めた。背景にあるのは「自分たちは物価高で苦しんでいるのに、大統領や周囲はその地位を利用して私腹を肥やしている」という国民の不満だ。今回の選挙は「左右」より「上下」の対立と言われるが、その構図が一段と鮮明になった。
The top five voter concerns are government corruption出典：Fox News　2026/10/14(水)
Democrats have made corruption a key midterm issue出典：MS NOW　2026/10/16(金)
トランプ大統領の純資産が1兆円を超えたという試算をアメリカの経済誌「フォーブス」が明らかにしました。出典：テレ朝NEWS　2026/9/18(金)
FOXニュースの調査では国民の約6割が「政府内の汚職」を「非常に懸念している」と述べ、インフレや移民問題などを上回り有権者の最大の懸念事項となった。トランプ氏に近いFOXの調査であることが、結果の信ぴょう性を高めている。
NBCニュースの調査では52%が「トランプ政権は過去の政権より腐敗している」と回答。ロイター通信の調査によると、共和党員も含めた国民の約7割がトランプ氏の私的な事業が大統領としての意思決定に影響を与えていると考えている。
ワシントン・ポスト紙は社説で「トランプ氏の家族や側近は富を蓄える一方、一般市民はインフレやガソリン価格の高騰に苦しんでいる」と批判。また「自身の支持者への恩赦や献金者への関税免除によって不正な資金提供の疑いを招いている」と大統領の汚職疑惑を指摘した。
フォーブス誌によるとトランプ大統領の直近の純資産は73億ドル。大統領選挙期間中の43億ドルの約70%増しだ。同誌は「米国史上いかなる大統領も、トランプほど地位を利用して巨額の利益を得た大統領はいない」と断じた。
こうしたトランプ氏の公私混同への国民の不満や批判が、自身の支持率低下と共和党のピンチを招いていることはほぼ間違いない。

title: トランプ氏支持率31% ロイター
body: Jason Lange[ワシントン　１９日　ロイター] - ロイター／イプソスの最新の世論調査で、トランプ米大統領の支持率が３１％と、２週間前から１％ポイント‌低下し、大統領１期目、２期目を通して最低水準となった。高騰するガ⁠ソリン価格に対する有権者の懸念が強まる中、１１月３日の中間選挙で共和党に厳しい審判が下される可能性が示された。「ジェネリ​ック・バロット（一般投票意向）」に関する項目の「きょう議会選挙が行われるとしたらどちらの党の候補に投‌票するか」との質問に対し、登録有権者の４７％が民主党、３５％が共和党と回答。民主党の１２％ポイントのリードは今回の選挙サイクルで最大となる。ジェ‌ネリック・バロット調査は、‌回答者がどちらの政党に連邦議会を主導し​てほしいと考えているかを測る全国調査。実際に上下両院の支配権を左右す‌る州別・選挙区別の選挙戦の詳細までは反映しておらず、共和党が制度的に優位な地域もある。２週間‌前のロイター／イプソス調査で​は、民主党が４４％、共和党が３７％で、民主党のリードは７％ポイン‌トだった。共和党の議会選候補への支持低下は、民主党に投票すると答えた女性の割⁠合が増えたことが主因だった。女性有権者の５０％が民主党に投票すると回答したのに対し、共和党候補への投票を考えているとの回答は３２％だった。男性も民主党を⁠支持する割合が共和党を上回ったが、その差は女​性より小さかった。ト‌ランプ氏の支持率は、２月に同盟国イスラエルとともにイランへの軍事攻撃を命じて以降、低迷している。戦争によってガソリン価格が急騰し、家⁠計が圧迫されている。トランプ氏の経済運営を支持しないと答⁠えた国民は６８％に上り、共和党支持者を自認する回答者でも３７％に達した。経済運営をより適⁠切に担える政党として、有権者の４０％が民主党を選び、共和党の３３％を上回った。調査は１９日まで４日間にわたり‌オンライ⁠ンで実施され、米国の成人１６７９人（うち登録有権者１２７９人）から回答を得た。​誤差は回答者全体でプラスマイナス２％ポイント、登録有権者でプラスマイナス３％ポイント。

title: 米国防長官 ネタニヤフ首相と会談
body: [エルサレム／ワシントン　２０日　ロイター] - ヘグセス米国防長官が１９日にイスラエルを電撃訪問し、ネタニヤフ首相とイラン情勢について協議した。イスラエル首相報道官‌が２０日、ロイターに対し明らかにした。ヘグセス氏もイスラエルを訪問し⁠たと確認したが、ネタニヤフ氏との非公開の会談の詳細について明らかにしなかった。イスラエルのシュピールマン首相報道官によると、ネタニヤフ首相はイスラエル南​部ネゲブ砂漠のウブダ空軍基地でヘグセス長官と会談。「地域の脅威」について協議し、その脅威に対し攻撃面と防衛面の双方で対処する米国とイ‌スラエルの協力について意見交換した。ヘグセス氏はイスラエルが米軍を受け入れていることに謝意を示したという。シュピールマン氏によると、駐留する米軍は数千人規模に上‌る。シュピールマン氏によると、両氏は‌トランプ米大統領によるネタニヤフ首相への支持についても意​見交換した。「両者の深い個人的関係が今回の協議の中心にあった」としている。ヘグセス氏はその後、ワシン‌トンで記者団に対し、イスラエルを訪問したと確認し「現地で米軍部隊を訪問し、その際に（ネタニヤフ）首相と話をす‌る機会があった」と語った。会談の​内容について話すことはないとし、「イスラエルが良きパートナーであ‌ることに感謝している」と述べるにとどめた。ヘグセス氏はこれに先立ち、ソーシャルメディアへの投稿で、中⁠東、北東アフリカ、アジアの一部を対象とする米中央軍の管轄域内で米軍将兵を訪問したと明らかにしていた。前日にはトランプ米大統領が、来週行われるイスラエル総選挙を巡りネタニヤフ氏への支持を表明。今⁠回の選挙は、２０２３年１０月７日のイスラム組織ハマスによるイスラエル奇襲攻撃​以降、初めてとなる。この攻撃‌を受けてイスラエルはパレスチナ自治区ガザ、レバノン、イランで戦闘を展開した。世論調査によると、ネタニヤフ氏率いる宗教・民族主義勢力の連立与党は過半数を失う見通しだ。ただ、野党側⁠も政権樹立に苦戦する可能性がある。バンス米副大統領は１９日、デジタルメディア「２ＷＡＹ」のインタ⁠ビューで、イスラエルの選挙には関与しないと述べ、ネタニヤフ氏への支持表明を控えた。「私が支持を表明す⁠るのは米国の候補者だ。私が注力しているのは中間選挙だ」と述べた。同氏は今年、ハンガリーのブダペストを‌訪問し、同国⁠の選挙でオルバン首相への支持を表明していた。バンス氏はネタニヤフ氏について、「​不支持を表明しているわけではないが、支持を表明しているわけでもない。イスラエルの選挙には関与しない」と語った。

title: SpaceXとテスラ 経営統合を検討
body: 米実業家イーロン・マスク氏は20日、自身が率いる米宇宙開発企業スペースXと米電気自動車（EV）大手テスラの経営統合の可能性を検討する特別委員会を設置したと明らかにした。欧米メディアが伝えた。マスク氏は両社の統合について「良いアイデア」と発言した。【写真まとめ】夜空に次々と現れたスターリンク衛星のフレア◇「シンギュラリティーの段階にある」この日のスペースXの決算説明会で言及した。報道によると、マスク氏は人工知能（AI）について「（人間の知能を超える）シンギュラリティーの段階にある」とした上で、両社の統合で得られるものは多いとの認識を示した。経営統合は「良いアイデアだと思うが、最終的には株主が支持しなければならない」と述べ、委員会はまだ合意に至っていないと強調した。◇マスク氏自身は議論に参加せずテスラ側は投票した株主だけでなく、全株主の50％の賛成票が必要になると指摘し、「かなり高いハードルだ」とした。マスク氏自身は利害関係にある当事者であるため、いずれの取締役会の議論にも参加していないという。【ワシントン浅川大樹】

title: ソニーFGへの立ち入り検査検討
body:
ソニー生命保険で総額数十億円規模の金銭不祥事が発生している問題をめぐり、金融庁は11月にも親会社のソニーフィナンシャルグループ(FG)に対して立ち入り検査を実施する方向で検討に入った。■内部統制や経営管理体制を問題視ソニーFGは2025年9月の再上場にあたって、傘下の損害保険事業や銀行事業、介護事業の機能を、付加価値の伸びが最も大きいソニー生命へ実質的に融合する「スクラム構想」を掲げてきた。その中核となるソニー生命で金銭不祥事が相次いでいることを受けて、金融庁はソニーFGの経営管理体制にも問題があるとの見方を強めている。
本記事はダイジェスト版です。金融庁が特に問題視している点について、そしてソニーFGの社長が元金融庁長官であることが及ぼす影響などについては、東洋経済オンライン有料版「〈独自〉金融庁がソニーFGに立ち入り検査を検討、中核のソニー生命で金銭不祥事相次ぎ管理体制を問題視」でご覧いただけます。

title: フラット35 全国で不適正利用64件
body: 長期固定金利型住宅ローン「フラット35」の融資審査について会計検査院が調べたところ、民泊施設や店舗として利用する不適正利用が計64件あったことが判明した。【図解】住宅はいま「売り時」で「買い時」?　金利上昇懸念の影響フラット35では、各金融機関が審査したうえで利用者に住宅購入資金を融資する。独立行政法人「住宅金融支援機構」は、金融機関からローン債権を買い取る証券化支援を実施するなど、住宅ローンの供給を支援することで国民の住宅取得を後押ししている。利用者は融資が受けやすくなる一方、購入した物件を事業で使わず、居住することなどが要件として求められる。検査院は2023～24年度に融資対象となった全国の5万4221件のうち、都市部の戸建て住宅を抽出調査。その結果、64件（融資額計30億4074万円）の不適正利用が発覚した。届け出をせずに住宅の一部を店舗などに利用したのが39件、民泊などに利用したのが25件だった。東京都豊島区の3階建ての新築戸建てでは、ローン利用者が8000万円の融資を受けたが、検査院が確認したところ、利用者は居住せず、物件を無許可で旅館業施設として使っていたことが発覚。この利用者の勤務先は、複数の旅館業施設を運営する会社だった。検査院は、64件のローン利用者が適切な対応を取らなければ全額繰り上げ償還などを求めるよう機構に要請。また、金融機関の融資審査時点で住宅の間取りを確認したり、民泊の届け出状況を確認したりする対応も求める。【山田豊】

title: 北海道職員が「就活セクハラ」か
body: 学生が参加する北海道主催のインターンシップで、道の男性職員が女子学生に交際を迫るなど不適切な連絡を繰り返していたことが20日、毎日新聞の取材で判明した。就職活動中の女子学生が被害に遭う「就活セクハラ」に該当する可能性があるとして、道は男性の処分を検討している。【図解でわかる】当てはまる？令和時代のハラスメント道によると、インターンは8～9月、道に就職を希望する大学生らを対象に開催し、計291人が参加。セクハラ行為が疑われている男性職員は所属部局でインターンに参加した学生の指導などを担当していた。男性職員は8月のインターンに参加した女子学生とLINE（ライン）の連絡先を交換。女子学生にメッセージを送り、食事に誘うなどした。女子学生は断ったが、男性職員はさらに連絡を重ねたという。女子学生が道の担当部局に相談して問題が発覚。道は女子学生に謝罪し、男性職員をインターン担当から外した。道は「事実関係を調査中」として、20日現在で男性職員を処分していない。男性職員は女子学生に対する行為についておおむね認めているという。道人事課の担当者は毎日新聞の取材に対し「参加した学生の期待を裏切る行為。再発防止に努めたい」とコメントした。【小林大輝】

title: VW  給与上昇30年まで凍結検討
body:
【ロンドン＝市川大輔】独自動車大手フォルクスワーゲン（ＶＷ）が、世界のグループ従業員６６万人の給与上昇を２０３０年まで凍結する方針を検討していることがわかった。現在の物価上昇の状況では、実質１０％超の賃下げとなる。経営再建につなげる狙いだが、労働組合は強く反発している。【表】20歳が欲しい車ランキング
ドイツ最大の産業別労組で金属産業などでつくる「ＩＧメタル」が１９日明らかにした。
ＶＷの経営側が世界中の人事担当者に対し、賃上げを停止するよう指示した。給与は２６年の水準を３０年まで据え置く計画という。
従業員団体は「経営陣のやり方はばかげている。給与を半減しても、車両コストの削減効果は５％にすぎない」との声明を出した。
ＶＷは中国メーカーとの競争激化などで業績が低迷している。３０年までに計１０万人を削減し、車種数を３５年までに半減するなどの構造改革を既に打ち出している。

title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
summary: Ukraine had accused the US of withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by Washington.
body:
Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff.
The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed.
Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday.
Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link.
A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps".
The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually.
Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions".
Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.
Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
Trump envoy Witkoff (L) joined Finnish President Stubb (C) and Zelensky (R) before their talks in Oslo
Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now".
"Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said.
He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia.
Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink.
Last week, a bipartisan group of US senatorscalled for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink networkin Ukraine.
And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war.
"Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.
The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.
Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
European leaders meanwhile have expressed concern about recent US statements from the US towards Russia.
On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".
"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.
Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".
"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
summary: France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday.
body:
Watch: Clean up begins after some of the worst disorder in France's modern history, but police remain
Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.
France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.
A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.
So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.
But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.
Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside.
Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors will come into force in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. An overnight curfew in parts of Paris, which came into force on Monday, has also been extended.
Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities – a place where generations of new arrivals have landed.
18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away.
"It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said.
Maryam (R) joined the protests on Saturday, which began in September over poor school conditions before escalating to cover broader issues such as the cost of living
Maryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops.
She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen.
"It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began.
"But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact.
"Sometimes it goes too far."
For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers.
"It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented."
Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La Canebière - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-Élysées - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north.
Hundreds of businesses were looted in several locations across the city
Blaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc.
"The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed."
I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses.
"That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured.
"Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat."
'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight
Watch: Shops looted and restaurants gutted in Paris riots
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening.
He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor Benoît Payan.
Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen.
"Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday.
He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics.
"If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again."
He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted."
Chantal Bellanger said she was worried for young people rioting out of anger and despair
While the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend.
At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time".
"We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned."
She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair.
"It tugs at your heartstrings," she said.
"To see children whose actions are going to place them completely outside of society. It's painful to watch."
Additional reporting by Paul Pradier and Pol Reygaerts

title: Man charged with attack on Australia MP to face court
summary: Brendan Nugent's family say they have known Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition, for more than 20 years.
body:
The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attack
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.
The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.
Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".
Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.
"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.
"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."
They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".
Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.
Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.
Helen Haines sits as an independent MP for the electoral division of Indi in Australia's state of Victoria
She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help.
A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies.
Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."
In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.
As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.
Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.
The community, and country, remain in shock.
At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.
Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.
One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.
body:
Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.
After theirnotorious televised bust up in the Oval Officein February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said thesanctions contained in the Graham Act(named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surroundsUkraine's access to Starlink.
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
summary: Revolut was one of the hardest hit, with banking services going down for many customers.
body:
Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.
The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.
Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.
The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.
"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.
"Services have been restored."
They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on itsservice health dashboard,external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.
Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.
In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.
It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.
These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.
The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.
Banks appeared to be among the most badly affected, with customers reporting problems ranging from being unable to access funds abroad to struggling to complete a property purchase.
Rachael Ellen, 25, a Revolut customer from Glasgow, told BBC News she was left unable to access her money.
"Today I was unable to pay for my parking at a shopping centre because my Revolut account wasn't working properly," she told the BBC.
"This left me in a difficult situation as I had no way to access the money I needed at the time."
She said the outage also meant she could not view a transaction from a relative and was told by the app's help bot that there were no pending incoming transactions.
"It's frustrating not knowing where the payment is or when I'll receive it," Rachael added.
Rachael Ellen said the outage caused her "real inconvenience" when she couldn't access her funds on Revolut
More than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services were flagged to platform outage monitor shortly after 08:00 BST on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company said some Revolut services were disrupted earlier as a result of the Google Cloud outage.
"We can confirm that services are now fully restored. Our customers' money and data are safe and remained safe throughout.
"We apologise for any inconvenience caused."
Customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by the Lloyds Banking Group - also reported issues affecting some online banking services.
A Lloyds spokesperson did not confirm the cause of issues affecting some of its services, but told the BBC later on Tuesday "we understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon".
Guy Baybutt, who works for a family-run business The Veg Box Company also said he was "severely affected" by Tuesday's outage.
Baybutt, who is from Preston, told the BBC the firm - which supplies fresh fruit, vegetables and other produce to customers across the UK - could not access its website to download and process customer orders amid the technical issues.
"We were also unable to book parcels onto DPD's system for collection, meaning orders that should have been dispatched today were at risk of being delayed," he said.
"To make matters worse, customers were unable to access our website to place new orders, meaning we lost valuable sales during the outage."
He said that such disruptions can have "serious financial consequences" for small businesses like his own.
"We don't have the resources of larger companies to simply absorb lost revenue, particularly when we're dealing with fresh, perishable produce that needs to reach customers promptly," Baybutt added.
Guy Baybutt told the BBC its services had recovered, but it was frustrating "that a technical failure completely outside our control brought so much of our business to a standstill"
Tuesday's incident came exactly one year after more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline for hoursduring an outage at AWS' largest cloud site.
Experts say this latest outage show how many businesses still rely on core services provided by a few large cloud operators.
"Google Cloud's outage is a reminder of how deeply our economies depend on just a handful of cloud providers," said Prof Feng Li, associate dean for research & innovation at Bayes Business School.
He added that it was not yet clear what caused the power problem identified by Google Cloud.
"Large cloud systems are complex, and failures will happen.
"What matters is how far they spread, how quickly services recover and whether customers have workable alternatives," he added.

title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
summary: The long-awaited decision about the controversial North Sea field is expected on Wednesday morning.
body:
The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North Sea
The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made.
The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months.
Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea.
Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw.
Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.
Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas.
The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government.
Licences for the fields weregranted by the Conservative UK governmentin 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups.
The Court of Session in Edinburghruled last yearthat Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.
Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.
They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.
Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
body:
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.
The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada  broke down in August.
The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.
The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
The White House has been contacted for comment.
Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.
Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.
The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.
That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".
The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carneymatched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar"after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.
It  also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.
Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.
The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.
"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.
The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.
It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)that were struck down in Februarythis year.
Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
summary: No formal investigation has started, but the regulator is making inquiries into the case.
body:
The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City.
The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September.
No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case.
It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than £900m. City are appealing the verdict.
The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs.
The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules.
It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies.
BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm.
The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme.
Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".
Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases.
He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules.
"This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account.
"The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability."
BDO declined to comment.

Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.
They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.
Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

title: Second Labour MP suspended over Covid loan repayments
summary: Perran Moon, MP for Camborne and Redruth, voluntarily referred himself for investigation.
body:
Perran Moon has referred himself to be investigated
A second Labour MP, Perran Moon, has been suspended over Covid loan repayments, after voluntarily referring himself for investigation.
Moon, the MP for Camborne and Redruth, is listed on Companies House as the co-director of atraining company called Autoswot,external, which last filed accounts in June 2021.
Government Bounce Back Loans of up to £50,000 were made available to support small businesses during the pandemic, but agovernment reportfound the scheme was vulnerable to fraud and error.
In August, Labour MP Bayo Alaba was suspended after queries about a Covid-era loan, and a third MP, James McMurdock, quit Reform in 2025 after questions about eligibility for loans he received.
Bounce back loans worth a total of £46bn were issued when the scheme was launched in May 2020, making it the biggest of the government's pandemic-era loan schemes.
Each one had a 100% government guarantee, meaning taxpayers' cash was used to pay back banks if the companies failed, but the Covid counter-fraud commissioner later found total fraud and error estimated at up to £2.8bn to the public purse.
Autoswot had been set up in June 2019, a year before the loans became available, and at that time had forecast revenues of more than £200,000.
Moon stressed he had applied for the maximum loan of £50,000 within the rules, regularly seeking professional advice about its obligations, and would provide documents to the Labour Party investigation into the matter.
He said the loan was used to pay for "staffing and other essential business costs" during the pandemic and partial repayments were made until the company ceased trading in late 2022.
The BBC understands that Moon was repeatedly assured in writing by Companies House that no accounts needed to be filed after the company applied to be struck off, but that guidance was incorrect.
Moon, who was first elected in the 2024 Labour landslide following a career in communications and marketing, said the business folded due to unforeseen external market pressures and "despite the best efforts of staff".
He said: "In order for these matters to be looked into, I have voluntarily referred myself to the Labour Party's investigations process and will cooperate fully with this process.
"The loan application was made in good faith, and the information provided, including the company's turnover forecast, was accurate and properly based.
"I will continue to work hard every day representing my constituents while this party process is ongoing."
A Labour Party spokesperson confirmed Moon had referred himself for investigation.
"The Labour Party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and we have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld," they said.
"We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing."
This is the second investigation the Labour Party has launched into the loans, withAlaba, the MP for Southend East and Rochford, also referring himself for investigation over loans made to a real estate company, Alaba Properties.
At the time, Alaba said: "There has been no attempt to avoid my financial obligations, and I am wholeheartedly committed to ensuring that the liability is met in full."
McMurdock, who now sits as an independent, was thefirst MP to be questionedover bounce back loans given to two fitness companies worth £70,000.
In 2025 McMurdock said all his business dealings had been compliant with the rules, adding that after taking "specialist legal advice" he had decided "to continue my parliamentary career as an independent MP".

title: Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch
summary: Speaking ahead of next week's Budget, the Conservative leader says her party would make £70bn of cuts.
body:
Kemi Badenoch has said Labour will not have the "courage" to make the public spending cuts she argued were necessary to bring down debt and fund defence.
Speaking in central London, the Conservative leader said the chancellor was hoping to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" next week but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible."
Highlighting her own plans to reduce spending by £70bn, Badenoch said: "Cuts are never easy but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair."
Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson described Badenoch's solution as "reverse Robin Hood politics – giving tax breaks to the wealthiest while offering nothing to ordinary people".
Chancellor John Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans on 28 October  - the first Budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister.
Healey has come under pressure to set out how he will boost defence funding to 3% of national income by 2030. However, this announcement is not expected until the government's spending review next year.
The Budget is also unlikely to include details about any changes to the welfare system, with those expected once former cabinet minister Alan Milburn produces his review into young people and work.
Badenoch said: "If Labour's plan is to kick tough decisions into the long grass, come out with tiny bits of micro-policy, put up a few taxes, spend a bit more on welfare, and hope nobody notices before the next election, they are kidding themselves."
The Tory leader noted that the International Monetary Fund (IMF)had recently praised the UKfor its plans to reduce its borrowing.
"The IMF clearly don't know this Labour Party like I do," she said.
She said Labour's plans required "huge cuts to the public sector" in 2029 and that the party would call an election before then.
"They are not suddenly going to find the courage to cut spending in the final year of a Parliament right before an election... Investors aren't buying these fictional cuts either."
Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor
Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
The most recentfigures showthat in August government borrowing stood at £18.3bn. The government is paying £8.8bn on its debt - the highest level since records began in 1997.
Badenoch said her party would reduce borrowing by finding £70bn of savings, including through cuts to the welfare bill.
Under her party's "golden economic rule", half of the savings would go towards reducing the deficit.
"Cuts are never easy, but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair," she said.
"Fair to taxpayers, fair to future generations, and fair to those who really do need support."
The Conservatives have recently announcedthey would scrap inheritance tax on family homesand allow couples to leave £1m tax-free.
The party has alsopledged to scrap a rule that sees parents in England earning more than £100,000 a year lose out on childcare support.
Asked if the Conservatives were the party for the rich, Badenoch told the BBC her policies would "help everyone".
"Quite frankly, getting people off welfare is doing something for them... the best welfare is a well-paying job," she said.
Pressed on whether she would make changes tothe triple lockto reduce the amount spent on pensions, Badenoch said she did not want to see "pensioner poverty" and that there were other things the party could do to grow the economy.
The trade unions and the Liberal Democrats have urged the government to raise money by putting a windfall tax on banks, who have reported large profits in recent years.
Badenoch dismissed this suggestion, arguing it would hit bank shareholders, including people's pension funds.
Setting out her party's policy Liberal Democrat leader Daisy Cooper said: "It's outrageous that while households have been grappling with the cost-of-living crisis, the big banks have benefited from a taxpayer-funded windfall worth billions."
She said the money raised from putting higher taxes on the bank could go towards reducing the cost of petrol and diesel and transport fares.
Reform UK economic spokesman Robert Jenrick challenged Healey to use the Budget to increase funding for defence, reduce benefit fraud and to make cuts to "foreign aid to rich countries" and "all the mad net-zero subsidies".
Speaking at a Reform rally in Plymouth, Jenrick added: "I suspect he won't. In fact, I confidently predict that this Budget will contain exactly what the last two did: tax rises again."
Responding to Badenoch's speech, Phillipson said: "Under the Tories debt rocketed, interest rates went up, while family finances and businesses were hammered.
"Labour has taken the fair decisions to reverse the Conservatives' decline. The economy is growing, interest rates have fallen, and private investment has returned.
"We're giving people breathing space on the cost of living and delivering everyday fixes to make life that little bit easier."

title: Farage vows to scrap tax on armed forces reserves
summary: A large group of protesters turned up outside the Reform UK rally in Plymouth with Nigel Farage.
body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage spoke at a rally in Plymouth
The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, has told a rally in Plymouth he would get rid of tax on pay for armed forces reservists.
Farage said he wanted to get more people in the reserves at the event for party supporters as part of Reform's 100 Days to Save Britain tour.
When questioned by the BBC over a Reform councillor in Plymouth who was investigated and cleared over social media posts, Farage said he was "still part of the party was because everyone believes he's a solid bloke".
About 100 protesters against Reform gathered outside the Plymouth Arena near the city centre, chanting before, during and after the event.
Reform leader Nigel Farage greeting supporters at the rally in Plymouth
Farage spoke to about 300 Reform members and councillors and opened his speech by paying tribute to Ann Widdecombe,who was killed at her home in Devon.
On cutting tax for reservists, he said: "Anyone that signs up as a reservist and does their bit will face no tax on the pay they receive.
"Let's get more men and women signing up for the reserves."
When asked by the BBC aboutthe UK deploying fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, Farage said the UK was "not even a player any more".
He said: "Should we help with peacekeeping missions? As much as we can.
"But what we've got to face up to is the reality that we've lost our ability to be an effective player".

Plymouth Reform councillor Ben Rowe was investigated in May afterbeing accused of sharing Islamophobic posts on social mediabut was then cleared.
The BBC asked Farage if Rowe's behaviour had been acceptable.
He said: "These are working class people, going into politics, venting their spleen on certain issues and maybe there's a little bit of political growing up to do.
"But let's not condemn everybody for everything they say, and the reason he's still part of the party is because everyone believes he's a solid bloke."
Pretesters against the rally gathered outside Plymouth Arena
Outside the event, amid a significant police presence, protesters gathered with placards and joined in chants saying Farage was not welcome in the city.
Liam Condron-Farnos, from the campaign group Stand Up To Racism, said: "The way he's built his politics over the years, and still is, is on anti-immigrant hysteria.
"We need to show him that's not an uncontested view in this country."

title: Government failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
summary: The sixth report from Covid inquiry criticises the lack of PPE and the way patients were discharged from hospital.
body:
Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said.
The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.
There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.
The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.
It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.
Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.
Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.
Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire".
"At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said.
"The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."
Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says
Covid inquiry PPE report - key findings
At the start of the pandemic, the then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock said the government had placed a protective ring around care homes.
But the report said that this claim was unfounded.
a lack of PPE meant staff had to resort to make-shift workarounds, including bins bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls
the decision to discharge hospitals patients into care homes at the start of the pandemic was understandable, but guidance should have made clear they needed to be isolated. This did not happen in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which was a significant oversight
a lack of financial support for care workers at the start of the pandemic made it difficult to allow them to stay away from their job if they were infected
long-standing weakness in the care sector, including financial struggles and staff shortages, exacerbated problems
by September 2020, evidence suggested care home visitors posed only a marginal infection risk, yet many care homes failed to ease restrictions in line with updated UK guidance, contributing to a significant decline in residents' health and wellbeing.
there was evidence of blanket do-not-resuscitate orders being put in place in some care homes, which is considered unlawful
millions of unpaid carers were left to take on evermore complex care and struggled because of a lack of support
Jean Adamson, of the Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK, said: "Today's report is a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country's history.
"It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing. Failing to act until it was too late."
Caroline, Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said the report was "devastating".
"When Covid took off, people using social care and the staff and unpaid carers providing it were left totally exposed."
She added it also demonstrated how important the overhaul of social care promised by Andy Burnham when he became prime minister was.
"If a national care service had already been in place... the various disasters that befell social care during the pandemic would have been lessened and some might have been avoided altogether."
Meanwhile, Natalie Grayson, from the GMB union, said care workers were "left vulnerable and terribly exposed" during the pandemic which saw "care homes turned into morgues".
"That cannot be allowed to happen again," she added.
Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers in England described the findings as "really upsetting", adding that the social care workforce has "never fully recovered" from the pandemic.
She said we need to "start thinking about social care in a more constructive way" and the mantra that "we all had to protect the NHS" appears to have come at the cost of "some care home residents' lives".
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government would provide a "full response" to the report's recommendations "in due course".
Speaking in the Commons, Cooper said she agreed that social care had been "undervalued and under-recognised" for too long.
"My thoughts are with all those who lost loved ones in the pandemic, and especially those who endured the immense distress and harm of visiting restrictions in care homes, which meant they could not be with loved ones even as they died," she added.
